column4: The wall was about to fall, so the servant “set it upright” (فَأَقَامَهُ), and Moses immediately speaks of taking a wage (أَجْرًا); one ayah directly joins the section’s straightened workpiece to the worker’s pay.

The command to set the face upright for religion joins Allah’s human fitrah/creation, the unchangeable creation, and “the upright religion” (ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ), exactly gathering the section’s fourth meeting.
This ayah itself joins embryonic shaping, maturity, being returned (يُرَدُّ) to the feeblest age, and dead soil swelling into life, and frames all of them as evidence for resurrection doubters.
People are “returned to Allah, their true Master” (رُدُّوا۟ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ مَوْلَىٰهُمُ ٱلْحَقِّ), and the same ayah declares that judgment is His, directly joining return and judgment.
The secure, tranquil town whose provision came abundantly then tastes hunger and fear after denying Allah’s favors is the section’s safe-provisioned city and its reversal in one scene.

Human beings stand (يَقُومُ ٱلنَّاسُ) before the Lord of all worlds after the surrounding weighing fraud and resurrection question, completing the section’s movement from assay to standing before the Judge.
The Book is قَيِّمًا and gives believers who do sound deeds “a good reward”; with the absence of crookedness in 18:1, this ayah directly joins straightness, righteous work, and recompense.

“What is with you runs out, and what is with Allah remains,” followed by recompense for patient people according to their best deeds, states the section’s passing-versus-uncut-wage meeting almost as a definition.
Everything perishes except Allah’s face, while judgment belongs to Him and all are returned to Him; passing, remaining, return, and judgment meet in one ayah.

Those who spend without following it by mann (reminding others of their favor) or injury retain their reward with their Lord; this Quranic sense of مَنّ sits directly beside the section’s “uncut reward.”

The command not to nullify charity through mann and harm, followed by the rain-stripped rock, turns a supposedly good work into one that leaves no yield, matching the rejected or spoiled workmanship in the section.
“Judgment belongs only to Allah” and “that is the upright religion” (ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ) place the two semantic workshops of حكم and قوم together.
The fixed measure of twelve months dates from Allah’s creation of heaven and earth, and the ayah calls this “the upright religion”; creation, temporal measure, and q-y-m religion meet directly.
The ayah commands judgment by revelation, urges competition in good works, and ends with everyone’s return to Allah, uniting the section’s judge, sound work, and return.
The just balances set for Resurrection weigh even a mustard seed and Allah suffices as reckoner, carrying the moneychanger’s exact assay into the divine court.
“Establish the weight with justice” (أَقِيمُوا۟ ٱلْوَزْنَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ) directly joins q-w-m uprightness to an undiminished scale.
Believers are called “the uppermost,” and Allah promises He will not diminish their deeds; height and work whose value is not cut down meet in the same promise.
Whoever “turns back from his religion” (يَرْتَدِدْ … عَن دِينِهِ) and dies faithless has his works rendered void, directly joining the r-d-d family’s apostasy sense to rejected work.
The idolaters “fabricate a lie” (تَخْلُقُونَ إِفْكًا), while their fabricated gods cannot provide; this is the human false-making sense of kh-l-q set against Allah’s real creation and provision.

The woman recommends hiring Moses because the best hire is “the strong, the trustworthy” (ٱلْقَوِىُّ ٱلْأَمِينُ), joining dependable strength to paid work just as the section joins emîn, the implement, and wage.
Belief and righteous deeds receive “a reward never cut off” (أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ), the exact formula whose lexical images the section unfolds.
Belief and righteous deeds receive “a reward never cut off,” exactly repeating the sixth ayah’s work-and-enduring-wage formula.
Allah directly promises the addressed Messenger “a reward never cut off,” preserving the exact phrase while changing the addressee from the faithful group to the Prophet.
The people made happy remain in the Garden and receive “a gift not cut off” (عَطَآءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ), a direct synonym-scene for the uncut wage.
Paradise provision is declared to have “no depletion” (مَا لَهُۥ مِن نَّفَادٍ), making perceptible the same refusal of exhaustion as غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ.
The Creator “created you, fashioned you, and balanced you”; 82:9 then turns from that careful making to denial of the Judgment, reproducing the section’s creation-to-dîn sequence.
Allah composes the human being in whatever form He wills; between the balancing of 82:7 and denial in 82:9, this ayah supplies the particular bodily form made by the craftsman.
“Yet you deny the Judgment” (تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ) follows the making and balancing of 82:7–8, exactly placing takdhîb against divine formation.
Allah “created and proportioned” (خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ), the direct parallel to the made and straightened human form; 87:3 adds measure and guidance.
Allah “measured and guided” (قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ), showing that the well-made form also has an assigned measure and direction, completing 87:2’s creation.
After the life stages and revived field in 22:5, this ayah states their inference: Allah is the Truth, gives life to the dead, and is capable of everything.
This ayah completes 22:5’s proof by naming the coming Hour and the raising of those in graves; it identifies what the revived field is meant to establish.
The hypocrites are in “the lowest depth of the Fire” (ٱلدَّرْكِ ٱلْأَسْفَلِ), the Quranic destination that gives the section’s spatial “lowest” reading its severe boundary.
Allah creates, causes death, and returns some people (يُرَدُّ) to the feeblest age until knowledge is lost, a direct repeated formulation of temporal return into bodily decline.
Whoever is granted long life is “reversed in creation” (نُنَكِّسْهُ فِى ٱلْخَلْقِ), stating without r-d-d the same bodily turn from upright strength toward decline.
Creation moves from weakness to strength and back to weakness and gray hair, making the rise-and-return arc of the human body explicit.
The ayah counts creation from dust and drop through maturity and old age, with some taken earlier, another full Quranic enumeration of the life scale developed in 22:5.
Every soul meets what it sent ahead, people are returned (رُدُّوا۟) to Allah their true Master, and their inventions vanish; the ayah joins assayed work, return, truth, and failed fabrication.
Allah has praise in both lives, judgment is His, and “to Him you are returned”; judgment and return are again assigned to the same hand.
The command to set the face toward “the upright religion” precedes a day that cannot be turned back from Allah, joining q-y-m religion to the boundary of return.
The question “Who is better than Allah in judgment?” opposes divine judgment to the judgment of ignorance, directly illuminating the closing question of surah 95.
The Book’s ayat are “made firm” (أُحْكِمَتْ) and then detailed by the Wise One, displaying the nonjudicial sense of h-k-m as work secured against defect.
Allah removes Satan’s insertion and then “makes firm His signs” (يُحْكِمُ ٱللَّهُ ءَايَٰتِهِ), a Quranic enactment of protecting work from corruption.
The Book contains “firmly established ayat” (ءَايَٰتٌ مُّحْكَمَٰتٌ), the root’s secured-construction side that the section places beside judging.
Believers who do sound works are assured that Allah does not waste the reward of one who makes work good, directly stating successful workmanship and preserved wage.
Worldly wealth and children are adornment, while “the enduring righteous deeds” are better in reward and hope, concretely joining what remains, sound work, and recompense.
“The enduring righteous deeds” are better in reward and “return” (مَرَدًّا), directly bringing lasting work, pay, and the r-d-d family into one line.
Believers are commanded to speak “a straight/right word” (قَوْلًا سَدِيدًا); 33:71 makes the consequence the repair of their deeds.
Allah will “make sound for you your deeds” (يُصْلِحْ لَكُمْ أَعْمَٰلَكُمْ), giving the section’s explanation of ṣāliḥāt as unspoiled work an explicit verbal form.
Those who denied their Lord’s signs and meeting have null works, so no weight is established for them on Resurrection; rejected work and failed assay meet directly.
Allah turns to the deeds people performed and makes them scattered dust, the clearest scene of apparent work being rejected as worthless.
The warning that association would nullify the addressee’s work sets a hard boundary around which work retains value.
A human being has only what he strives for; 53:40–41 then show the work inspected and paid in full, like a craft presented for assay.
The striving “will be seen,” supplying the inspection between labor in 53:39 and full recompense in 53:41.
The inspected striving is repaid with “the fullest recompense,” completing the work-and-full-weight wage scene.
Whoever does an atom’s weight of good sees it, joining minute weight to the visibility and recompense of work.
Whoever does an atom’s weight of evil sees it, giving the divine scale its opposite pan and its judgment boundary.
The House is made “a place of return and security” (مَثَابَةً … وَأَمْنًا), joining sacred place, coming back, and safety immediately before Abraham’s provision prayer.
Abraham asks that the town be secure and that its believing people be provided fruits, exactly the two qualities the section assigns to the sworn city.
Abraham and Ishmael raise the House’s foundations and ask that their work be accepted; beside 2:125–126, sound construction, acceptance, safe place, and provision form one scene.
Abraham asks Allah to make this land secure; 14:37 supplies the sacred valley and requested fruits, repeating the safe-city prayer.
Abraham places descendants by the Sacred House in an uncultivated valley and asks that they receive fruits, joining sacred location, barren ground, worship, and provision.
The objection that guidance would cost the Meccans their land is answered by the safe sanctuary to which fruits of every kind are gathered as provision.
People see that Allah made a secure sanctuary while others are seized around it, yet they believe falsehood and reject His favor; safety and denial face each other directly.
The command to worship “the Lord of this House” fixes the source of the feeding and security named in 106:4.
Allah feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear, the concise positive counterpart to the reversed town in 16:112.
Abraham’s standing-place is among the House’s signs, and whoever enters it is secure, joining the sacred locale to both qiyām imagery and safety.
Allah made the Kaaba “a support/standing for people” (قِيَٰمًا لِّلنَّاسِ), bringing the secure sacred place into the q-w-m family that holds the human form upright.
Moses perceives a fire while traveling and turns toward it; 28:30–31 transform that distant fire scene into divine address and safety from fear.
The call comes from the blessed side of the valley by the tree, locating the divine meeting between the fire of 28:29 and the reassurance of 28:31.
Moses turns away in fear when the staff moves and is told to return, approach, and be among the secure (ٱلْءَامِنِينَ), explicitly staging fear’s change into safety at the fire encounter.
The woe to fraudulent measurers opens the commercial assay scene that ends with people standing before the Lord in 83:6.
The fraudsters demand full measure when receiving from others, supplying the self-serving standard behind the section’s sound and faulty money.
When measuring or weighing for others they cause loss, the direct opposite of a full-weight dinar and just judgment.
The question whether the defrauders expect to be raised turns the market scale of 83:2–3 toward the final standing of 83:6.
The command to give full measure and weigh with “the straight balance” (ٱلْقِسْطَاسِ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمِ) is the Quranic counterpart of the full-standard coin and straight shaft.
“Give full measure” and do not cause loss introduces the just commercial standard completed by the straight balance in 26:182.
“Weigh with the straight balance” (ٱلْقِسْطَاسِ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمِ) directly joins straightness and full assay.
Scripture and the balance are sent so people may “stand for justice,” and iron has mighty force; q-w-m, equitable measure, judgment, and the crafted metal implement meet here.
One person entrusted with a treasure returns it, while another entrusted with a dinar does not; the ayah joins the section’s dinar, trust, and return in a commercial test.

The brothers find “our merchandise returned to us” (بِضَٰعَتُنَا رُدَّتْ إِلَيْنَا); unlike the section’s defective dirham, this commercial return restores value and provision rather than rejecting it.
Noah’s people “denied the messengers”; 26:107 calls Noah trustworthy and 26:109 places his wage with the Lord, giving the denial side of the section’s endurance-trust-wage triangle.
Noah says, “I am to you a trustworthy messenger” (رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ), between his people’s denial in 26:105 and his divine wage in 26:109.
Noah asks no wage from the people and assigns his wage only to the Lord of the worlds, completing 26:105–107’s denial and trust scene.
ʿĀd “denied the messengers”; 26:125 and 26:127 answer that denial with a trustworthy messenger whose wage is with Allah.
Hūd’s claim to be a trustworthy messenger supplies the dependable side opposite ʿĀd’s denial in 26:123 and beside his wage statement in 26:127.
Hūd asks no wage and places his wage with the Lord, completing the repeated denial-trust-unfailing-pay pattern.
Thamūd “denied the messengers”; 26:143 and 26:145 supply the trustworthy messenger and his Lord-held wage.
Ṣāliḥ says he is a trustworthy messenger, the stable claim set against denial in 26:141 and joined to divine wage in 26:145.
Ṣāliḥ asks no wage and reserves his wage to the Lord, completing another exact recurrence of the section’s linked images.
Lot’s people “denied the messengers”; 26:162 and 26:164 place a trustworthy messenger and his wage across from that denial.
Lot declares himself a trustworthy messenger, directly opposing his people’s denial and preceding the statement of his wage.
Lot asks no wage from his people and places his wage with the Lord, completing the trust-denial-wage refrain.
The people of the thicket “denied the messengers”; 26:178 and 26:180 supply Shuʿayb’s trustworthiness and divine wage.
Shuʿayb says he is a trustworthy messenger, the reliable side of the denial named in 26:176 and the wage named in 26:180.
Shuʿayb asks no human wage and places his wage with the Lord, closing the surah’s repeated denial-trust-pay structure.
Hūd asks no wage and says his wage rests only with the One who originated him, directly joining reward to real creation.
Allah “made good everything He created” and began human creation from clay; 32:9–11 proceed through bodily fashioning, denial, death, and return.
Allah fashioned the human, breathed spirit, and made hearing, sight, and hearts; the careful making is followed by ingratitude and resurrection denial in 32:10.
People ask whether, once lost in earth, they can be in a new creation; this denial stands between divine formation in 32:9 and return in 32:11.
The angel of death takes people and then they are returned to their Lord, answering 32:10’s denial and completing formation, descent into earth, and return.
The human created from a drop becomes an open adversary, directly turning real creation into the stance that disputes resurrection.
The denier forgets his own creation and asks who can revive decayed bones, staging the broken body that divine making must restore.
The answer is that the One who originated the bones the first time will revive them, opposing remembered real creation to the denier’s claim.
The human asks whether he will be brought out alive after death; 19:67 answers denial of return with first creation.
The human is reminded that Allah created him before when he was nothing, making first creation the answer to denied resurrection.
Allah asks whether first creation wearied Him and identifies the deniers’ confusion about a new creation, directly placing making and doubt face to face.
“We created you; why do you not affirm?” turns human creation into the same pointed question that surah 95 directs at denial.
Allah decrees death among people and cannot be outstripped, beginning the return side of the creation argument in 56:57–62.
Allah can replace people with their likes and create them in a form they do not know, linking bodily form to divine power over return.
Knowledge of the first creation is made the reason to remember and accept the next, completing 56:57’s creation question.
The human doubts that Allah will gather his bones; 75:4 answers with the even finer precision of restoring fingertips.
Allah is able to proportion even the fingertips, carrying the section’s exact bodily workmanship through death and reassembly.
From a clot Allah “created and proportioned” the human, the same creation-and-straightening pair, before 75:40 asks about reviving the dead.
The rhetorical question asks whether the One who fashioned the sexes is not able to revive the dead, matching surah 95’s closing argumentative stance.
The embryo passes through measured forms into bones clothed with flesh and another creation, displaying the workmanship later carried through death and rising in 23:15–16.
After the formed creation of 23:14, human beings die, the downward break before 23:16’s raising.
After death, people are raised on Resurrection Day, completing the formed-body, ending, and restored-standing sequence.
The human is commanded to consider what he was created from, opening a creation argument whose conclusion in 86:8 is Allah’s power to return him.
After naming the fluid from which the person was made, the ayah says Allah is able “to return him” (رَجْعِهِ), directly linking creation to return.
The question “From what did He create him?” begins a compact life sequence that reaches measured formation, death, burial, and resurrection.
Allah creates the human from a drop and measures him, joining material creation to deliberate proportion.
Allah causes the human to die and places him in a grave, the groundward stage between measured creation and raising.
When Allah wills, He raises the buried human, completing the creation-to-ground-to-standing movement.
The question recalls creation from a lowly fluid; 77:22–23 place it for a measured term and 77:24 confronts deniers.
“We determined, and excellent are We at determining” makes exact measure the divine work immediately before the warning to deniers.
“Woe that day to the deniers” follows the created and measured embryo, another compressed meeting of formation and takdhîb.
Allah’s layered creation contains no inconsistency, and the viewer is told to return the gaze to seek a crack, like a finished work subjected to inspection for defect.
The gaze is returned twice and comes back humbled and weary, unable to find the defect; repeated return confirms the Maker’s flawless work.
Allah created in truth, formed people, and made their forms good, then names the final destination to Him; fine formation and return share the ayah.
Allah makes earth a settlement and heaven a structure, forms people and makes their forms good, then provides good things; workmanship, place, and provision meet directly.
Rain is driven to “a dead land” (بَلَدٍ مَّيِّتٍ), brings out fruit, and is explicitly likened to bringing out the dead, joining the balad family’s soil face to resurrection.
Allah brings living from dead and dead from living, revives earth after its death, and says people will be brought out likewise.
The reader is told to look at how Allah revives earth after death; the same reviver will revive the dead, making the field a direct resurrection proof.
Winds and clouds revive a dead land, and the ayah concludes “such is the resurrection,” repeating 22:5’s field-to-rising inference.
The humbled earth stirs and swells when water descends; its reviver is declared able to revive the dead, a close nonlexical repeat of 22:5.
Measured water revives a dead land, followed by “thus will you be brought out,” joining measure, provision, earth, and resurrection.
Rain-provision revives a dead land and is followed by “thus is the emergence,” making food from earth a figure of human rising.
Humans are created from earth, returned into it, and brought out from it again, the complete bodily descent-and-rising movement in one ayah.
Allah caused human beings to grow from the earth like growth; 71:18 supplies their return into it and renewed emergence.
Allah returns people into earth and brings them out anew, explicitly turning burial ground into the route of restored creation.
The earth is made a gathering container, and 77:26 specifies that it holds both living and dead bodies.
The earth contains “living and dead,” giving the section’s place-family image its graveward bodily face.
An oath by “this city” begins a surah that says in 90:4 “We created the human,” a striking structural parallel to surah 95’s city oath and human creation.
“We created the human in toil” supplies the human condition after the city oath of 90:1, parallel to surah 95 while replacing best proportion with struggle.
Sincere worship, prayer, and alms are named as “the religion of uprightness” (دِينُ ٱلْقَيِّمَةِ); 98:7–8 then connect righteous work to created rank and lasting reward.
Faithless deniers are called the worst of creatures, the low side of the rank whose opposite appears with righteous workers in 98:7.
Believers who do righteous deeds are called the best of creatures, joining work to the restored human rank opposite 98:6.
The best creatures receive their reward and abiding gardens, completing 98:5–7’s upright religion, sound work, rank, and enduring recompense.
Humanity is declared in loss, the general downward condition from which 103:3 exempts believers and righteous workers just as 95:6 does.
The exception for those who believe, do righteous works, and uphold truth and patience closely parallels the exception from human descent in 95:6.
Sheba receives two gardens and the invitation to eat the Lord’s provision in “a good land”; 34:16–17 show this provisioned place reversed by refusal and ingratitude.
When Sheba turns away, the flood replaces its two productive gardens with bitter and sparse growth, staging provision’s withdrawal from a favored place.
The reversal is explicitly called recompense for ingratitude, making the ruined provision an assayed outcome rather than an arbitrary fall.
Settlements on the journey are made visible and travel in them is secure by night and day; 34:19 shows this durable safety undone by the people’s demand.
The people ask that their journeys be lengthened, wrong themselves, and are scattered, reversing the secure measured road of 34:18.
Had the towns believed and been mindful, blessings from heaven and earth would have opened; because they denied, they were seized, joining belief, denial, provision, and reversal.
Satan promises to command people to alter Allah’s creation; this is the explicit hostile boundary against 30:30’s unchangeable fitrah and divinely set form.
Believers are told not to weaken or grieve because they will be “the uppermost,” the faith-conditioned reversal of being brought to the lowest.
Iblis’s proud claim to height is answered, “descend” and be among the abased, showing a moral descent in which self-exaltation produces lowness.
At the descent from the garden, Allah promises that whoever follows His guidance will neither go astray nor suffer, a guided boundary within the downward movement.
Whoever turns from the reminder receives a constricted life and is raised blind, the opposite outcome to the protected followers in 20:123.
The one whose scales are heavy enters a pleasing life, beginning a direct weighed-outcome contrast completed by 101:8–9.
The one whose scales are light receives the opposite verdict to 101:6, making deficient weight itself the turning point.
The light-scaled person’s refuge is the abyss, joining failed weight to literal downward destination.
Faces are “working, exhausted” (عَامِلَةٌ نَّاصِبَةٌ) yet enter fire in 88:4, the hard opposite of sound work receiving an uncut wage.
Other faces are pleased with their striving, the successful counterpart to the exhausted but rejected labor of 88:3.
Garden fruit is “neither cut off nor forbidden,” a concrete paradisal opposite to the section’s rope, lifespan, milk, and traveler images of interruption.
Paradise contains rivers of milk whose taste never changes; this stable milk reverses the section’s dictionary image of kezebe, milk that fails before its expected term.
Worldly goods are temporary enjoyment and adornment, while what is with Allah is better and more lasting, stating the two sides of depletion and endurance.
Worldly provision is temporary enjoyment, while what is with Allah is better and more lasting for believers who trust their Lord, joining permanence to faith and reliance.
People prefer the nearer life; 87:17 answers that preference with the better and more lasting afterlife, the section’s short-lived versus enduring line.
The afterlife is “better and more lasting,” directly naming the enduring side opposite the preferred nearer life of 87:16.
The Prophet is guided to a straight path and “an upright religion” (دِينًا قِيَمًا), another Quranic use in which q-w-m describes religion rather than a body or tool.
Whoever turns back from religion (يَرْتَدَّ … عَن دِينِهِ) will be replaced by a people Allah loves, another explicit apostasy sense of the section’s r-d-d family.
The warning says obeying the faithless would turn believers back on their heels, so they would return as losers; bodily reversal figures religious reversal.
Disputed matters must be “referred back” (فَرُدُّوهُ) to Allah and the Messenger if people believe, using r-d-d as the route to authoritative judgment.
Allah promises the return of all to Him and then His judgment concerning their differences, a close non-r-d-d parallel to return and divine adjudication.
Whatever people differ about has its judgment with Allah, to whom the speaker turns and upon whom he relies, joining adjudication and directed return.
Noah appeals to Allah’s true promise and calls Him “the wisest/best of judges” (أَحْكَمُ ٱلْحَٰكِمِينَ), the exact closing title placed in a concrete plea for judgment.
Shuʿayb asks his two opposed communities to wait until Allah judges between them and calls Him the best of judges, giving the closing title a communal dispute scene.
The Messenger is told to follow revelation and remain patient until Allah judges, “the best of judges,” turning the title into a stance of waiting under pressure.
Judah resolves to remain until his father permits him or Allah judges for him, and names Allah the best of judges; the formula governs a painful family impasse.
Believing migrant women are not to be returned to the disbelievers, and the rule is immediately called Allah’s judgment between the parties, joining nonreturn and الحكم in one legal scene.
Shuʿayb commands his people to give full measure and weight and not diminish people’s goods, a commercial version of sound, unrejected value.
Shuʿayb confronts a people whose practice concerns measure and weight; 11:85 supplies the positive command to make both full and just.
The command to fulfill measure and weight with justice and not diminish goods gives the moneychanger image an ethical standard.
The command to fulfill measure and balance with justice extends exact assay into covenantal conduct.
After full measure and a straight balance, the people are forbidden to diminish others’ things or spread corruption, explaining what faulty assay does socially.

Joseph is sold for a few counted dirhams, a Quranic coin scene in which human beings themselves are drastically undervalued; the link is to the section’s dirham and assay image, not to a counterfeit coin.
The father offers Moses marriage in exchange for eight or ten years of labor, supplying the actual term and payment behind the trustworthy hire of 28:26.
Game within reach of hands and spears tests who fears Allah unseen; the section’s straight spear appears here as a functioning implement whose use exposes the worker’s obedience.
Moses tells his family he perceives a fire and will bring news or a burning brand; 27:8–10 turn the sight into a divine meeting and reassurance from fear.
Moses turns in flight from the moving staff and is told that messengers need not fear in Allah’s presence, repeating the fire encounter’s fear-to-safety turn.
Moses perceives a fire and hopes to bring a brand or guidance from it; 20:11–12 reveal that the apparent fire has led him to the sacred valley and divine call.
The called Moses is told he is in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā, grounding the fire scene in the mountain-place invoked by surah 95.
People count their Islam as a favor (يَمُنُّونَ), but Allah says the true favor is His guidance to faith; this distinct m-n-n sense tests who can claim credit for belief and reward.
The command not to give or confer favor seeking increase uses the m-n-n family in an action-and-return setting, a different sense from “uncut” reward that guards work from self-interested accounting.
The promised garden has food and shade that are دائم, a concrete picture of provision that does not run out.
The Prophet must not strain toward temporary worldly splendor; the Lord’s provision is better and more lasting, another explicit endurance boundary.
The people of the lasting abode say neither weariness nor fatigue touches them, answering the section’s dictionary picture of the exhausted traveler stranded on the way.
Moses’s servant says their journey has brought them fatigue (نَصَبًا); it concretely stages the weary traveler used in the section to explain a life or reward being cut short.
The observer is shown bones being raised and clothed with flesh, a resurrection scene that answers the section’s dictionary image of a bone’s faulty or repaired joining.
Allah creates death and life to test who is best in deed, joining created mortality to the quality-assay of human work.
Allah creates the human from a clinging form; 96:8 later identifies the return to the same Lord, giving another compact creation-and-return span.
“To your Lord is the return” closes the challenge to the self-sufficient human who was reminded of creation in 96:2.
The secure person is asked whether he feels safe from the earth swallowing him, making bodily descent the boundary of presumed security.
The next question asks whether one feels safe from a storm sent from heaven, completing the warning that worldly security can be withdrawn.
Many settlements exulting in their livelihood are destroyed and their dwellings left nearly uninhabited, a broad repeated scene of provisioned place reversed.
Feeding on a day of hunger gives concrete righteous work inside the city-oath surah, countering the hunger that clothes the ungrateful town of 16:112.
Feeding a poor person “in dust” places the low, earth-clinging body within the upward moral path of the city-oath surah.
After freeing and feeding, the climbers of the steep path are those who believe and counsel patience and mercy, another belief-and-work exception after human toil.
The exhausted workers of 88:3 enter a blazing fire, completing the reversal of labor whose outcome is punishment rather than enduring wage.

The ayah pictures extending a cord toward heaven and then cutting it; it may recall the section’s lexical explanation of m-n-n through a severed rope, though the ayah’s difficult image serves a different argument about frustrated rage.
